#9773. A Space Heater Is the Hardest Question You Can Ask a Smart Plug

The most dangerous product pairing in a smart home catalogue is also one of the most common: a 1,500-watt space heater and a smart plug sold as handling 15 amps. On paper the arithmetic works. In practice the heater sits at the plug's continuous load limit for hours at a time, and hours are what the rating was never about. Smart plugs fail on heaters not because the rating is a lie but because the rating answers a different question than the one a heater asks.

Electrical ratings for switching devices distinguish peak load from continuous load, and the difference is thermal. A relay contact passing 15 amps heats up. A kettle asks for 15 amps for three minutes, and the heat dissipates before it accumulates. A heater asks for 12 amps for six hours, and heat accumulates the whole time: the contact, the solder joints, the PCB traces, and the enclosure all climb toward a steady-state temperature that a short-cycle product never reaches.

Standards reflect this. Wiring rules derate continuous loads to 80 percent of a breaker's rating precisely because sustained current is harder than switched current. A plug rated 15 amps peak is, in that framing, a 12-amp continuous device at best, and a 1,500-watt heater on a 120-volt circuit draws 12.5 amps. The numbers meet exactly at the line, and the line is where thermal ageing lives.

The failure is not dramatic. The contact resistance rises as the contact material oxidizes and springs relax under thermal cycling. Higher resistance means more heat at the contact, which accelerates the oxidation, which raises the resistance again. The plug keeps working through the whole decline, which is what makes it dangerous: a plug that clicks and heats for a season, warms its own enclosure measurably, and one day stops conducting or worse does not.

The measurable warning signs exist for people who look. A plug body noticeably warm to the touch after an hour of heater duty. Discoloration around the socket. A relay click that has grown softer or occasionally fails to switch the load the first time. Any of these on heater duty is a replacement, not an observation.

The specifications that separate a heater-capable plug from a kettle-capable one are rarely the headline amperage. Continuous rating at ambient temperature, not just peak. Relay contact material and whether it is rated for high inrush and sustained resistive load. Thermal protection: a plug that measures its own temperature and cuts off at a threshold has a future; a plug that has no idea how hot it is does not. Enclosure material and its heat deflection point. Whether the manufacturer publishes a duty-cycle or derating curve, because a vendor who does has tested the question a heater asks.

Metering matters too, but differently than buyers assume. Energy monitoring does not make a plug safer; it makes the decline visible. A plug that reports its own power draw will show the heater drawing what the heater draws, and a sophisticated one can report temperature. For a load that fails by slowly cooking itself, telemetry is the difference between a scheduled swap and a surprise.

The heater problem has structural solutions worth preferring. A heater with its own thermostat and tip-over protection needs a dumb socket, not a smart one; the intelligence is already in the appliance. Hardwired heater control belongs on a switch or relay rated for the continuous load with headroom, ideally in the wall, where a failure is containable. Where scheduling is the goal, the schedule belongs in the heater if it has one, or in a device deliberately chosen for continuous duty.

If a smart plug must carry a heater, the selection rules are strict: continuous rating with margin, thermal cutoff, a name-brand contact specification, and a periodic inspection habit. Treat the plug as a wear item with a service life measured in heater-seasons, and replace it on schedule rather than on failure.

Small heaters change the arithmetic: a 600-watt oil radiator draws 5 amps, inside the continuous envelope of a decent plug with margin to spare. The rule is not that heaters and plugs never mix; it is that the mix needs continuous ratings, not peak ones. Decide from the wattage plate on the appliance, not the amperage on the plug's box, and leave headroom for the heater's own thermostat cycling.

The procurement questions are about sustained duty, not the amperage on the box. What the continuous rating is at realistic ambient temperatures. Whether the relay is specified for sustained resistive loads and what its electrical life is at that load. Whether the plug measures its own temperature and what it does at the limit. What derating the manufacturer publishes. What the failure mode has been in fleet deployments, if the vendor will say.

A plug family that answers these is designed for the loads people actually plug in. A family that quotes 15 amps and stops is designed for kettles and marketing. The difference is invisible on a 3-minute kettle boil and decides whether the same plug survives a winter on a heater, which is where the whole category quietly gets tested anyway.

#9771. FOC Vector Control in Vertical Robotics: Torque Ripple Suppression and Gravity-Compensated BLDC Drives

Most wheeled robotic platforms operate on horizontal planes where motor loads are symmetric and predictable. In vertical robotics, however, continuous downward gravitational acceleration creates severe torque asymmetries between upward climbing, downward braking, and lateral traversing cycles.

Traditional trapezoidal 6-step commutation generates significant torque ripple and mechanical vibration. When amplified against a thin glass pane, this vibration compromises negative suction stability and causes rapid track slippage. To achieve smooth surface adherence and precise velocity control, modern vertical platforms rely on Field-Oriented Control (FOC) algorithms executed on embedded ARM Cortex or specialized motor-control microcontrollers.

Field-Oriented Control (FOC) Implementation on Vertical Loads

Field-Oriented Control decomposes the stator currents of a 3-phase Brushless DC (BLDC) motor into two decoupled orthogonal vector components:

The Direct axis current (Id), controlling the magnetic flux linkage.

The Quadrature axis current (Iq), controlling the dynamic torque output.

By maintaining Id at zero and precisely modulating Iq via Clarke and Park transformations, the controller achieves smooth, maximum torque-per-ampere output. On a vertical glass pane, this continuous torque modulation minimizes micro-vibrations, ensuring the vacuum sealing lip remains completely flush against the surface at all times.

Sensorless Position Estimation vs. Magnetic Encoders

Determining rotor angle at zero or low speeds is critical when initiating a climb on steep glass:

Hall-effect sensors offer coarse 60-degree electrical resolution, which is insufficient for ultra-smooth low-speed positioning under heavy load.

Modern high-reliability platforms utilize high-resolution magnetic rotary encoders (such as 14-bit absolute angle sensors) communicating over SPI with the motor MCU.

In cost-optimized units utilizing sensorless architectures, microcontrollers deploy High-Frequency Injection (HFI) or sliding mode observers to extract rotor position from Back-EMF signals without requiring physical sensors in the harsh, humid cleaning chamber.

Asymmetric Drive Dynamics and Gravity Compensation

When traversing horizontally across a large glass pane, the upper and lower drive wheels experience radically different physical friction loads:

The lower wheel absorbs the full dynamic weight of the chassis plus tether tension.

The upper wheel tends to experience slight traction reduction due to chassis tilt.

The motion control loop integrates a real-time Gravity Compensation Vector derived from the 6-axis IMU:

Feed-forward torque offsets are calculated continuously at 1 kHz control loop frequencies.

If the optical surface encoder detects micro-slipping (a discrepancy between commanded rotor revolutions and actual displacement), the FOC loop immediately throttles Iq to recover traction before track decoupling occurs.

Evaluating motor drive stability requires continuous bench testing under variable friction coefficients, such as transition zones between dry glass, surfactant-treated glass, and framed edge silicone. Key hardware benchmarks include:

Total Harmonic Distortion (THD) in phase currents during abrupt vertical-to-horizontal trajectory switches.

Acoustic noise profiles and decibel ratings under heavy vacuum suction versus low-power traversal.

Real-world mechanical thermal dissipation across H-bridge MOSFETs during continuous 60-minute runs.

For comprehensive hardware teardowns, motor drive architecture comparisons, and empirical bench data across current commercial vertical robotics, explore the technical reports and motor performance datasets published at Window Robot Lab:https://windowrobotlab.com/

Are you implementing Field-Oriented Control (FOC) or sensorless BLDC drivers in your robotics projects? How do you handle torque ripple compensation under dynamic external loads? Share your controller schematics and algorithm insights in the comments below.

#9769. 4 Wonderful Signs You Have A High IQ

Four things that indicate high intelligence in a person.

Four things that indicate high intelligence in a person.

Being open to experience, cooperative, happy and having strong perceptual skills are all signs that you have a high IQ, psychological research finds.

Of these, being open to experience is a particularly strong sign…

Insatiable curiosity, an active fantasy life, a sensitivity to emotions and an appreciation of art and beauty are all linked to high IQ.

These are all aspects of the major personality trait called ‘openness to experience’.

People who are open to experience are more interested in things that are complex, new and unconventional.

Being open to experience is so powerful that it is linked to intelligence when measured almost 40 years later.

Children who scored higher on IQ tests at just 11-years-old were more open to experience when they were 50-years-old, the psychologists found.

Intelligent people are better at cooperating with others.

While personality traits like being generous and conscientious have an effect on cooperation, higher IQ is the main factor that encourages people to work well together.

People with higher intelligence use more consistent strategies and consider the consequences of their actions.

That is why people with high IQs are so essential: without them society would not work.

The finding goes against the popular idea that being intelligent somehow predisposes people to unhappiness.

The study looked at happiness in the best-known sense of feeling positive emotions and being satisfied with your life.

The results showed that people with the lowest IQ (70 – 99) were the least happy in comparison to those with the highest IQs (120 – 129).

People with high IQs have stronger basic perceptual skills, research finds.

For example, they can tell which way objects are moving more quickly.

They are also better at blocking out background information to make their judgement.

Imagine a ball thrown at high speed — a more intelligent person can pick up its trajectory faster.

A higher IQ makes the brain faster at a fundamental level.

It helps underline that high IQ is about more than just solving puzzles or making the ‘right’ decision.

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9768. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)


If you want to pay online, you need to register an account and provide credit card information. If you don't have a credit card, you can pay with bank transfer. With the rise of cryptocurrencies, these methods may become old.

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain. 

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

So, What is Blockchain?

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

  • Blockchain collects information in “blocks”.
  • A block has a storage capacity, and once it's used up, it can be closed and linked to a previously served block.
  • Blocks form chains, which are called “Blockchains.”
  • More information will be added to the block with the most content until its capacity is full. The process repeats itself.
  • Each block in the chain has an exact timestamp and can't be changed.

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

How does blockchain work?

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

Here’s how it works:

  • Someone or a computer will transacts
  • The transaction is transmitted throughout the network.
  • A network of computers can confirm the transaction.
  • When it is confirmed a transaction is added to a block
  • The blocks are linked together to create a history.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

  • A new transaction is added to the system. It is then relayed to a network of computers located around the world. The computers then solve equations to ensure the authenticity of the transaction.
  • Once a transaction is confirmed, it is placed in a block after the confirmation. All of the blocks are chained together to create a permanent history of every transaction.

How are Blockchains used?

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

What is Blockchain Decentralization?

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Pros and Cons of Blockchain

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages. 

Pros

  • Accuracy is increased because there is no human involvement in the verification process.
  • One of the great things about decentralization is that it makes information harder to tamper with.
  • Safe, private, and easy transactions
  • Provides a banking alternative and safe storage of personal information

Cons

  • Data storage has limits.
  • The regulations are always changing, as they differ from place to place.
  • It has a risk of being used for illicit activities 

Frequently Asked Questions About Blockchain

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Is Blockchain a cryptocurrency?

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Is it possible for Blockchain to be hacked?

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

What is the most prominent blockchain company?

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Who owns Blockchain?

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

What is the difference between Bitcoin and Blockchain technology?

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency 

What is the difference between Blockchain and a Database?

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Final Saying

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. #9767. How Crypto Wallets Are Becoming More Than Just Wallets

At the beginning of Bitcoin, there was no such thing as a crypto wallet as we know it today. You had a full node, took care of complex private keys, and that was it. A lot has changed since then. Simpler and lighter apps appeared over the years, making it easier for users to manage their coins. But the evolution didn’t end there: now, crypto wallets are more than just wallets.

These versatile apps can do a lot of things beyond just storing funds, signing transactions, and sending payments. Of course, it always depends on the brand and network(s) involved, but we can find many interesting features to take advantage of in numerous crypto wallets. Let’s explore some of them.

Historically, people's "identity"—even in the digital realm—has always been assigned and managed by third parties (governments, corporations, etc.). However, the decentralized world offers an alternative through the self-sovereign identity (SSI) model. As the name implies, this is a form of identity or personal verification that can only be managed by the user who owns that identity.

In this way, very specific data can be shared only when necessary, rather than all personal information—for example, only age is verified, and the name is never revealed. Some crypto wallets can handle this type of digital ID already, in different ways. In an SSI setup, the wallet generally stores the credential and its cryptographic keys on the user's device. The issuer creates and signs the credential, while a decentralized network may store a DID (decentralized identifier), public key, credential schema, or revocation/status information that helps verify it.

When the user presents the credential, the recipient checks the issuer's signature and relevant on-chain data without needing the credential itself to be public. Examples of wallets that already have this feature include Dock Wallet, cheqd Wallet, Privado ID Wallet, and the Obyte Wallet. In the latter, you can verify your real name, your email, your GitHub account, your status as an accredited investor by the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), and more.

All of this is done via chatbots integrated into the same wallet. Then, the information is stored in your wallet, and you can selectively share parts of that information with whoever you like.

You can't communicate directly with your transaction peers in every crypto wallet, but you can in some of them—and with end-to-end encryption, too. You can even send messages on-chain, if you want, and enjoy some easier chatbots here and there. Depending on the system, messages may travel through a peer-to-peer network and be read only by the intended recipient, and never by someone else.

As for more public on-chain messages that will last forever, this can be done even on Bitcoin, but it’s not exactly user-friendly there. The process often involves converting your message to hexadecimal code, finding specific wallets that support this function or advanced features inside wallets, and pasting that hex code into a designated field, sending a transaction without funds. In other crypto networks and wallets, it’s just a matter of writing whatever you want in a user-friendly menu, pressing “send,” and paying a small transaction fee.

Chatbots aren’t that common, but they can be welcome, especially for beginners. They can respond to commands or help users perform actions from a familiar chat interface. They can be related to Large-Language Models (LLMs) like Plug Wallet or KaleidoSwap, or simply follow ingrained instructions without the risks associated with AI, like the Obyte Wallet. In the latter one, you can enjoy all of these features: encrypted chat, user-friendly on-chain messages, and classic chatbots.

These days, it’s rare that your crypto wallet can’t interact with smart contracts and make programmable transactions. Smart contracts are small computer programs stored in a certain ledger and designed to carry out specific, pre-set rules. They can automate payments, exchanges, loans, bets, games, and many other applications.

In practice, when you’re inside a crypto wallet, the most you will typically see regarding a smart contract is the permission requested by a specific Dapp to connect to your address and, likely, use some of your funds. Unless you are a developer, you probably have little idea how to "read" one—let alone create one. Most wallets won’t show you this, either, but there are some of them with friendlier smart contracts.

Obyte is one of them. You can create conditional payments and smart contracts in human language inside the app, all of it without coding and via encrypted chat.

Besides, if you’re sending a transaction or interacting with a Dapp, you’ll be able to see a clear preview of the results and fees before pressing “Send” or “Pay.”

Remember the familiar routine of creating a new account for every website? Wallet-based authentication offers another route. With Sign-In with Ethereum (SIWE), for instance, a user can prove control of an account by signing a message. The signature happens inside the wallet, while the application verifies it. The standard was designed to give Ethereum accounts a consistent way to authenticate with services outside the network itself.

This can make one on-chain account useful across multiple applications. The address acts as a persistent identity that can be used across many Dapps, with the wallet handling the signature needed to prove control. Beyond MetaMask for Ethereum, other providers of this feature include Para and WalletConnect for multiple networks.

Beyond your own businesses, you can also contribute to your community and help shape the future of your favorite networks by participating in governance. On-chain governance lets token holders vote on proposals whose results can trigger changes to a network’s rules, parameters, treasury, or other functions. The voting process and its powers vary from one network to another, but the wallet can provide the place where users review proposals, connect their address, and cast a vote with their governance tokens.

The mechanics can be quite simple. A proposal appears in a governance interface, the wallet shows the vote and any required transaction, and the user confirms it by signing. Some systems use delegated voting, so users can assign their voting power to another address instead. In other cases, holding a specific token or meeting a balance requirement determines who can participate.

Examples include MetaMask supporting governance voting through compatible Dapps, Keplr providing governance features for Cosmos networks, and Obyte allowing users to participate in on-chain voting through its wallet and governance website.

In the end, the word “wallet” is starting to sound a little undersized for all of this. The same account can connect a person to applications, support communication, authenticate access, interact with programmable software, and even decide on the future of a network. A crypto wallet remains a place to manage digital assets, but its role can extend much further, and it'll likely continue to do so.

#9765. Your Free Server's Local Disk Is Not a Database: Five Persistence Myths and a Restart Probe

You deployed it. It worked. Then the instance restarted overnight.

Now your chat endpoint answers as if the conversation never happened. Was that disk supposed to hold your state?

This is a myth-busting FAQ about persistence on small, free-hosted apps. It ships with a restart probe you can run in about ten minutes. All code below is a template; I am not publishing measured results for your host.

The claim. fs.writeFile is durable, so a local JSON file is fine storage.

Why it feels true. It survives your process crashing. That is real.

What to check. Does the instance keep its disk across a restart? Across a rebuild? Those are different events. Ask your host explicitly, and reread the storage docs.

Corrected model. Local disk is scratch space with a marketing problem. Treat it as a cache you cannot trust.

The claim. If the disk survived last time, it will survive next time.

Why it feels true. You restarted the service and your files were still there.

What to check. A redeploy often builds a fresh image on a fresh machine. A restart may reuse the old one. Your test must name which event it exercised.

Corrected model. Restart, redeploy, and resize are three separate experiments. Run all three, or stop claiming durability.

The claim. Losing a warm cache is fine, because the cache warms itself.

Why it feels true. In steady traffic, yes, it does.

What to check. What happens on the first request after a cold start, with five hundred users arriving at once? That is a thundering herd, not a cache miss.

Corrected model. A cold cache is a load event. Budget for it, or gate the refill.

The claim. A sessions.json on disk is a fine interim solution.

Why it feels true. On a single instance, it is trivially simple and fast.

What to check. Restart the box while a user is mid-conversation. If the session vanishes, users see a forgotten session and a fresh greeting. They blame the model.

Corrected model. Local-file sessions are a single-instance lock-in. Fine for a demo, dishonest as a default.

The claim. I log every prompt and response to app.log, so I can debug later.

Why it feels true. The file exists, and it grows.

What to check. Restart, then look for the file. If it is gone, your audit trail had a lifetime measured in uptime.

Corrected model. A log on ephemeral disk is a debugging aid for the current boot, nothing more.

Stop asking "is it stored?" Start asking "where does it live, and what kills it?"

The rule I use: anything a user would notice missing goes in the bottom row. Everything else may live above it.

Here is the probe. Standard library only, no dependencies.

The one rule that makes or breaks this test. PROBE_LEDGER must point outside the instance. Put it on your laptop, in paste buffer output you capture, or in any store that does not die with the box. A ledger on the same disk proves nothing.

Three runs, three answers. Now you know which event eats your files. Do not guess.

If your app calls a model, the only record of what the model saw is the journal you wrote. Lose it, and you cannot explain a bad answer later.

So extend the probe. Log a prompt hash and a response hash per call, to the same external ledger.

Hashes keep the ledger small and avoid storing user text. You lose readability, and you gain the ability to prove a call happened. That trade is usually the right one for a prototype.

Why hash instead of skip? Because "the model gave a weird answer" is unfalsifiable without a record. Twelve hours after a restart, your log is gone and so is your argument.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

This probe is cheap to run and cheaper to run repeatedly. That is where a free server option and free model access genuinely help: you can host the tiny probe app, drive it with real model calls, and repeat the restart cycle without a paid round trip each time.

What this does not give you: any promise about durability, uptime, or retention. Availability of a free tier says nothing about persistence. That is exactly why you probe.

If you want to run this loop yourself, the free server option on MonkeyCode is enough to start, as long as you bring your own off-box ledger.

Not "where did I write it?" Ask "what kills this, and have I watched it die?"

Run the probe once. If it prints MISSING, you just saved yourself a confusing support ticket. If it prints SURVIVED, you now have evidence instead of a feeling.

#9762. Chrome Extension Compromised: A 3-Phase Response Checklist

Posted on Nov 6 • Originally published at extensionbooster.net

Originally published on ExtensionBooster.

If your Chrome extension is compromised, a malicious update can reach your users within hours, because Chrome checks installed extensions for updates "every few hours." In December 2024, one phishing campaign got into at least 35 extensions with more than 2.6 million users. Here is a response plan in three phases (first hour, first day, first month) that you can copy into your repo before you ever need it.

Two-step verification is not enough on its own. These are the three routes that keep coming up:

The clearest warning sign is a version in the Developer Dashboard that you never built. Other signs: Google emails about submissions you didn't make, users reporting new ads, redirects or permission prompts, and a sudden run of one-star reviews that mention malware.

You can automate the first check. This script asks Chrome's update service which version it is serving and fails if that doesn't match your latest release tag. The response format isn't a documented API, so treat it as an early warning, not a guarantee.

Run it on a schedule in CI and send failures to a channel someone actually watches at night.

Contain it first and investigate later. Keep a timestamped log of every step you take.

Unpack the rogue package and diff it against your last good release. Look for:

Then rotate any secrets that shipped inside the extension and invalidate sessions on your backend.

Your public notice should say what happened, which versions were affected and when, what they could access, what users should do now, and what you are changing. Your clean release can show the notice only to users who updated from an affected version:

Reply to every angry review with the same short, factual message: confirm the incident, name the fixed version and link to the notice. Don't argue, and never ask anyone to change their rating.

Keep the private key out of your Google account and out of every repo. If you lose it, Google says getting a replacement through support can take up to a week.

Your rating can recover. Since Google's August 20, 2026 update, the Chrome Web Store rating focuses on more recent reviews. A burst of one-stars hurts fast, but steady good reviews after the fix count for more than they used to.

The full guide, including a copy-paste checklist and FAQ, is in the Chrome extension incident response plan on ExtensionBooster. There are more growth and trust guides for extension developers in the ExtensionBooster developer resources.

#9761. 2 Personality Traits Linked To A Stronger Immune System

Certain personality traits influence the body’s immune system response.

Certain personality traits influence the body’s immune system response.

People with more stable emotions have stronger immune systems, research finds.

People who are emotionally stable usually find it easier to control their urges and are mostly unselfconscious.

Emotional stability is linked to being better at dealing with stress and minor frustrations.

Neuroticism lies at the opposite end of the spectrum from emotional stability.

People who are neurotic typically experience more negative thinking and tend to have worse mental health.

The study included 84 people whose response to a vaccine for hepatitis B was tested.

The results showed that people who were more neurotic — meaning easily stressed, nervous and moody — tended to have weaker immune system responses.

Those who were more emotional stable had a stronger immune response.

Dr Anna L. Marsland,, the study’s first author, said:

“The present findings support a link between trait negative affect and an objective health measure — antibody response to vaccination — raising the possibility that individuals high in trait negative affect or neuroticism may have less protective immune responses.”

In a second part of the study, people were given a stressful task to test their immune function.

The results showed that stress tended to lower people’s immune system response — as previous studies have found.

Along with emotional stability, extraversion has also been linked to a stronger immune system, by a genetic analysis.

Extraverts are typically outgoing, talkative and energetic, meaning they tend to interact with more people.

They are, therefore, exposed to more infections.

A stronger immune response may help to protect extraverts against infectious diseases.

Introverts, meanwhile, tend to have a weaker immune response, as do cautious people.

The study included 121 people who were given personality questionnaires, along with genetic tests and general health screening.

The results showed that extraverts had the highest expression of pro-inflammatory genes.

The effect of these genes is to help fight off infections.

Introverts and cautious conscientious people tended to have a lower inflammatory response.

The study was published in the journal Health Psychology (Marsland et al., 2001).

#9757. The Common Vitamin Linked To Weight Loss

The vitamin deficiency linked to increased belly fat.

The vitamin deficiency linked to increased belly fat.

Higher levels of vitamin D are linked to reduced belly fat, research shows.

The conclusions come from a study including thousands of people.

The researchers measured people’s total body fat and abdominal (belly) fat, along with their vitamin D levels.

The results showed that for both men and women vitamin D deficiency was linked to increased belly fat.

However, for women, low vitamin D levels were linked to both increased belly fat and increased total body fat.

For men, though, low vitamin D levels were linked to more belly fat and more liver fat.

More than half of people around the world may be deficient in vitamin D.

Dr Rachida Rafiq, the study’s first author, said:

“Although we did not measure vitamin D deficiency in our study, the strong relationship between increasing amounts of abdominal fat and lower levels of vitamin D suggests that individuals with larger waistlines are at a greater risk of developing deficiency, and should consider having their vitamin D levels checked.”

It is not yet known if low vitamin D levels are causing more fat to be stored or are a result of it.

“Due to the observational nature of this study, we cannot draw a conclusion on the direction or cause of the association between obesity and vitamin D levels.

However, this strong association may point to a possible role for vitamin D in abdominal fat storage and function.”

Vitamin D deficiency has also been linked to cardiovascular diseases, autoimmune diseases and a higher chance of getting colds.

Foods that are rich in vitamin D include oily fish and eggs, but most people get their vitamin D from the action of sunlight on the skin.

That is why levels are typically lower in the body through the winter months in more Northern climes.

The study was published in the journal Clinical Nutrition (Rafiq et al., 2018).

#9756. Small Tweaks, Great Output: What Merchants Can Do to Maximize Pay By Bank Conversion

Noda is an Open Banking technology provider.

Noda is an Open Banking technology provider.

Noda is an Open Banking technology provider.

Open banking payments are a genuinely good deal for merchants. Lower transaction fees than cards, near-instant access to settled funds, no card chargeback headaches. But in many markets, it's still a relatively new checkout option, and even where the infrastructure is mature (think the UK, the Netherlands or Germany), plenty of shoppers still default to what they know – cards, PayPal or other methods. In Central and Eastern Europe, awareness is growing fast, but it's still an education curve.

So how do you nudge your users to pick it? There are two ways to get there.

Some solutions, like Noda’s BIN-to-Bank, use smart routing through the card form to bring Pay by Bank into the payment flow without any changes to your checkout UI.

But if Pay by Bank is a visible option in your checkout, how it’s presented makes all the difference. We asked Lucy Oganisian, Product Designer at Noda, to share a few practical UX tweaks that can help merchants improve Pay by Bank conversion – whether you're running a WooCommerce store on a plugin that allows basic customisation or engineering a fully custom checkout from scratch.

Here's what actually works, tested and approved by our team.

Tests show that vague labels quietly kill conversion. Button names like "Bank transfer" or "Open Banking" leave users uncertain about what they're actually doing – and uncertain users don't convert.

“Pay by Bank” is becoming a recognizable standard in the same way "Pay by Card" is. Moreover, when "Pay by Card" and "Pay by Bank" sit next to each other, the choice feels obvious and balanced, not like one is the main event and the other is a footnote.

The same applies to localised checkouts: clear and direct translations tend to perform better than more creative alternatives.

When a payment method is unfamiliar, users look for anchors they already trust. Bank logos are one of the most powerful trust signals you can add, and they cost nothing to display.

A small row of recognisable bank marks near your Pay by Bank option signals two things: this is real, and my bank is probably here. That second part matters a lot. Users want to know their specific institution is supported before they proceed further.

Some providers like Trustly or Klarna push their own branding at this touchpoint, but that tells users very little if they've never heard of them. Familiar bank marks work like trust badges but more credible – because they're institutions users already rely on.

Hiding the Pay by Bank option below the fold is a pain point that hits hardest on mobile. If users need to scroll to discover it, it becomes the "backup plan" option, not a first choice. And that's exactly how it'll convert.

A couple of things to avoid: placing it out of the visible area on load, and creating multiple equally prominent buttons on one screen. When users face two "main" actions, they hesitate.

As for where exactly to put it: in markets where Pay by Bank is already a well-known checkout option, don't hesitate to place it first. In markets where awareness is still building, second position works nicely – visible and clearly labelled but not demanding attention before the user is ready.

Placing individual bank buttons directly into your checkout can be a great way to minimize further screens and potential drop-offs – especially for e-commerce flows.

But there's a ceiling. In many European markets, the top 3–5 banks cover roughly 70–90% of users, so a short preview serves the majority without cluttering the experience. Showing, for example, 5 banks tends to outperform showing 9: decisions feel easier, the flow stays pleasant, and conversion follows. The rest can live behind a "show more" option – accessible, but out of the way.

It’'s best to pick button colours that are consistent with your website. If the Pay by Bank button style clashes with your site's design – users notice, even if they can't articulate why.

The same goes for typography: text that fails to meet WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) requirements can easily become unreadable, often due to low contrast or font size. It excludes some users and signals a lack of polish to the rest.

If you're using a plugin and your provider offers customisation features, spend a few minutes on the appearance settings after setup. It's among the quickest, highest-return things you can do.

None of this requires significant technical investment. But these details do shape how Pay by Bank is perceived at checkout. Pay by Bank is often viewed as an attractive option for merchants. A few thoughtful tweaks can make it the more obvious choice for their customers too. What often determines uptake is how naturally the option appears in the user journey. When Pay by Bank feels visible, trustworthy and well-integrated, customers are far more likely to choose it.

#9753. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing

Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!

An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

#9743. The best apples for apple pie: Here's how to choose.: We put six varieties to the test.

Which are the best pie apples? With apple-picking season hard upon us, it's time to dust off your favorite apple pie recipe, sharpen your crust-rolling skills, and get ready to enjoy fall's favorite dessert: apple pie.

You may be tempted to make your pie from one of the six apple varieties that dominate the domestic market year-round: Red Delicious, Golden Delicious, Gala, Fuji, Granny Smith, and McIntosh.

But when fall rolls around, farmers' markets and orchard farm stands offer an abundance of apple choices.

You've probably identified your favorite eating apple. But what about the best pie apples? They're not necessarily the same. Red and Golden Delicious, for instance, are reliably crisp, sweet-eating apples. But when you bake them into a pie, they can become mushy and lose some of their sweetness. So what are the best apples for pie?

We'll put six different pie apples to the test.

The pie apples: I decide to put two of my favorites, Golden Russet and Northern Spy, up against a couple of classic pie apples: McIntosh and Cortland. I also add Granny Smith because, if there's one ubiquitous, year-round apple, Granny Smith is it. Ginger Gold — a Golden Delicious cross with Albemarle Pippin — is another variety that's often available in fall, and a worthy representative of the Delicious family.

And yes, there are plenty of other apple varieties to choose from: Fuji, Gala, Honey Crisp, and so many more. But with limited time and resources — and a pan with space for just six pies — I'm not able to test every apple out there. But if you want to choose the best pie apples among your personal favorites, you can have fun doing this same test at home.

I use a muffin tin to bake apples sweetened with a bit of sugar. To mimic apple pie (sans crust), I pile sliced apples high in the pan. Then I bake them in a preheated 425°F oven for 20 minutes, lower the oven temperature to 375°F, and continue to bake the apples until they're bubbly, about 40 minutes.

I had no idea there'd be such significant differences in both texture and flavor. For example, Russets and Macs are sweetened with the same amount of sugar, bake at the same temperature, for the same amount of time —  and offer way different results.

So, Granny Smith looks like the best combination of both taste and texture. Does it make the very best apple pie?

Not necessarily. I've baked many pies with this all-purpose apple, especially during the winter when other apples are scarce or pricey. A pie made 100% with Granny Smith apples is a mighty fine pie. But in fall, when every apple variety in the world is seemingly at your fingertips, why not take advantage of one or two (or more) of your own local favorites?

At the end of the day, choosing the best pie apples is a personal decision. My best apple pie would include a combination of these three: Cortland, for flavor; Russet, for texture; and Granny Smith, for its combination of the two.

What apples would fill your best pie? Bake your favorite varieties side by side and see what happens; the results may surprise you.

Please share your favorite apples for pie — and your favorite apple pie tips! — in comments, below.

#9741. 3 Personality Traits Associated With Infidelity

Up to 50% of people admit cheating on their partner.

Up to 50% of people admit cheating on their partner.

People who are low on conscientiousness are more likely to cheat on their partner, research finds.

People who are not conscientious are careless, badly organised and find it hard to resist temptation.

People who are more extraverted are also more likely to cheat on their partner, the researchers found.

It is probably because extraverted people have a wider social circle and so more opportunities to cheat.

Also, extraverts are impulsive, sensation-seekers who can easily succumb to their desires.

The conclusions come from a survey of 208 people, who were asked about their relationships and whether they had cheated.

Up to 50% of people admit cheating on their partner, the authors write:

“Early studies reported that by the age of 40, 50% of all married men and more than 25% of all married women have engaged in extramarital sexual behavior.

Three decades later, an estimated 50% of men continued to engage in sexual and/or emotional extramarital relations while 40% of women engaged in similar relationships.”

The results of the study revealed that cheaters tend to be low in conscientiousness, extraverted and open to experience.

Extraverts tend to seek out stimulation, the authors write:

“Extroverts may be inclined to cheat to obtain stimulation and prevent boredom.

Extroversion may also facilitate less investment in the relationship when those with this trait seek out others for stimulation, thereby decreasing commitment and resulting in cheating behaviours.”

The third personality trait associated with infidelity is openness to experience.

Openness to experience is linked to intellect and creativity.

“…cheaters may perceive themselves as having stronger intellect and stronger creativity compared to that of their partners, leading them to seek out partners that may be a better, that is, similar, match.”

The study was published in the journal Current Psychology (Orzeck & Lung, 2005).

#9738. How to prebake pie crust — and why you should: The key to flaky — not flabby — pie crust.

A soggy bottom. Not something you want for your baby. Or your pie crust. And while we can’t help you with your baby, there’s a simple solution to pies with soggy bottoms: prebake (also known as blind bake) the crust.

There are a number of reasons your pie can end up with a soft, pale, underbaked crust — and steps you can take to help prevent that unfortunate result.

But the one surefire way to make certain your pie’s crust will be golden brown, crisp, and delicious — just as appealing as its filling — is to prebake it. That’s right: bake the bottom crust first, before adding the filling.

Most commonly, it's smart to prebake pie crust when:

But some fillings might instead cook fully on the stovetop, like the rich, thick filling for chocolate cream pie. When it’s done, you simply pour it into its crust — and said crust had better be prebaked to perfection, since the pie’s not going anywhere near an oven.

Other pies, typically those with a more delicate, egg- and cream-based filling (think custard pie or quiche) require at least some baking — but don’t spend long enough in the oven (at a high enough temperature) to guarantee a fully baked, brown and crispy crust.

In these cases, you need to prebake your crust.

The recipe you're following may explain explicitly how to prebake your crust. But if it doesn't, follow this process:

First, roll your bottom crust and place it in the pan. Crimp or flatten the edge. Chill it for 30 minutes, to relax the gluten and firm up the fat(s); this will help prevent shrinkage, so don't skip!

Line the crust with foil, parchment, or a paper coffee filter. Fill it about two-thirds full with dried beans, uncooked rice (or other uncooked grain berries), pie weights, or granulated sugar.

Bake the crust in a preheated 375°F oven for 20 minutes, set on a baking stone or steel if you have one. Remove the crust from the oven and lift out the liner and weights. (If you’ve used sugar, save it for your future baking; it’ll be lightly toasted and yummy!)

At this point your crust is partially prebaked, and good for any of your pies that tend to exhibit a wan, flabby bottom crust when done. Think pumpkin pie: You don’t want to bake the filling so long that it’s stiff and dry, but you may pull your pie out of the oven to find your perfectly baked filling is resting in a partially baked crust. Prebaking your crust partway is a sensible solution for this scenario.

To fully prebake the crust, prick the bottom all over with a fork to prevent bubbles. Return the crust to the oven and bake for an additional 20 to 25 minutes, until it’s golden all over.

If, despite your best efforts, the lined, weighted crust still slips down the inside of the pan while it prebakes, try this: Bake the crust upside down.

To start, you’ll need two identical (or nicely nestable) pie pans with flat rims.

Place your rolled-out crust in one of the pans, anchoring it to the rim of the pan with a fork-tine crimp. Place a liner of some kind (same as above: parchment, foil, coffee filter) into the pan. Nest the second pan into the first.

Pick up both pans, turn them over, and set them on a baking sheet. Place the baking sheet and pie pans in the oven, and bake as directed above. As the crust bakes, gravity will pull it down toward its rim — rather than into a puddle at the bottom of the pan. Magic!

After 20 minutes remove the baking sheet from the oven, carefully turn the pans over, lift out the empty pan, and remove the liner. At this point, your crust is partially prebaked. To prebake it fully, place the crust back in the oven, right side up, and bake until it's golden.

If you struggle with a pale, pasty bottom crust in your fruit pie, then yes, you can prebake it — with a couple of caveats:

So, soggy bottoms begone! From now on I expect every pie you bake will have a deep golden brown, flaky, crispy crust on the bottom — all because of the prebake.

And if you have any other questions about pie — from creating tender, flaky crust to thickening fruit filling to assessing when your pie is perfectly baked — please check out our Pie Baking Guide.

#9736. 2 Supplements That Significantly Reduce Heart Disease And Cancer Risk

The most recent trial confirms that two nutrients can reduce deaths from heart attacks and cancer.

The most recent trial confirms that two nutrients can reduce deaths from heart attacks and cancer.

Omega-3 fatty acids from fish oil can significantly reduce heart attacks and vitamin D supplementation can significantly lower the number of deaths caused by different types of cancer.

Researchers studied 26,000 American adults in the VITAL clinical trial for five years to see if fish oil or vitamin D would definitely ward off cardiovascular disease or cancer.

The outcomes were reassuring: marine omega-3 fatty acid intake was linked to a significant drop in heart attacks.

One-and-half servings per week of dietary fish intake showed the maximum heart health benefits, but higher dietary fish intake didn’t help more.

The greatest decrease in heart attacks was seen in African-Americans.

The benefit of 1 gram of omega-3 fish oil supplementation showed a small decrease in major cardiovascular events like stroke and death from cardiovascular disease.

Vitamin D3 or cholecalciferol intake at a dose of 2000 IU per day showed a significant decrease of death from cancer for those who took it for at least two years.

However, supplementation with vitamin D3 capsules didn’t significantly lower incidence of any type of cancer or cardiovascular disease.

Dr. JoAnn Manson, the study’s first author, said:

“The pattern of findings suggests a complex balance of benefits and risks for each intervention and points to the need for additional research to determine which individuals may be most likely to derive a net benefit from these supplements.”

Dr. Stephanie Faubion, NAMS medical director, said:

“With heart disease and cancer representing the most significant health threats to women, it is imperative that we continue to study the viability of options that prevent these diseases and help women survive them.”

The 1 gram omega-3 fish oil supplementation used in the VITAL clinical trial was Omacor, a prescription medicine for adults.

The capsule contains 840 milligrams marine omega-3 fatty acids, of which 465 mg is eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and 375 mg is docosahexaenoic acid (DHA).

The study was presented at the North American Menopause Society (NAMS) Annual Meeting in Chicago (Manson et al., 2019).

#9734. How long does pie last in the fridge? : Because we're all wondering what to do with our apple and pumpkin pies.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions. Today: How long does pie last in the fridge?

The season of plentiful pies is upon us. When preparing several pies for a holiday meal, you may be wondering about the imminent leftovers. Should apple pie be stored differently than pumpkin pie? David from our Baker’s Hotline is here with his expert advice to help.

“Baked apple or other fruit pies can be kept covered, at room temperature, for one to two days. After that, they’ll keep in the fridge for one to two more days,” David advises. A 15-minute reheat in a 350°F oven can help revive some of that freshly baked flavor. Tent the pie with foil so it doesn’t brown further.

Interested in prepping ahead? David says that storing an assembled, ready-to-bake apple pie is a bad idea; the fruity filling will release moisture, which will make your crust soggy. Instead, roll out your pie crusts and prep your apples, but keep them separate. And wait to add the sugar and spices to the apples until you’re ready to bake the pie. This way, you can pour off any liquid that’s accumulated from the fruit without draining off your thickener, sugar, and spices.

Sliced apples turn brown, so you don’t want to keep your prepared apples in the fridge very long before baking. Aim for under 24 hours, but a squeeze of lemon juice could help them last another day or so.

And if you want to use your freezer to prep ahead, here’s how to freeze and bake fruit pies.

David advises, “Baked pumpkin pie or other pies containing eggs and/or dairy such as pecan pie, custard pie, or chiffon pie should be stored refrigerated; they’ll keep in the fridge for three to four days. I like to transfer the pie to a shallow, lidded storage container, but plastic wrap or a storage top can be used as well.”

As with apple, if you’re making your pumpkin (and other custard) pie ahead, it’s best to keep filling and crust separate. Pumpkin pie filling can be made ahead; it’ll keep, refrigerated, overnight. In fact, that's actually what we recommend doing; the custard develops incredible flavor and aroma as it sits.

If you can, serve pies the day they were made instead of refrigerating them.

Reheat refrigerated pies in a 350°F oven for about 15 minutes prior to serving.

Apple and other fruit pies will last at room temperature for up to two days, then in the fridge for two more.

Pumpkin, custard, or other egg/dairy-based pies can be stored in the fridge for up to four days.

If you’re making the crust and the filling ahead, keep them separated until it’s time to bake your pie.

Get more tips for holiday success in our Thanksgiving Baking Guide.

#9731. This Vitamin Reduces Mental Health Problems By 50%

Around half the world’s population are thought to have an insufficiency of this vitamin.

Around half the world’s population are thought to have an insufficiency of this vitamin.

A triple dose of vitamin D3 supplementation in the first two years of life reduces the chance of mental health problems later on by around 50 percent, a high-quality experiment finds.

Infants who were given 30 µg of vitamin D daily, which is three times the recommended dose, were only half as likely to have internalising problems by age 6-8.

Internalising problems are those in which a person keeps their problems to themselves, including depression, anxiety, loneliness and withdrawal.

Dr Samuel Sandboge, the study’s first author, said:

“Our results suggest that a higher dose of vitamin D3 supplementation during the first years of life may reduce the risk of internalizing psychiatric symptoms in late preschool and early school age.”

The randomised controlled trial, which was carried out in Finland, was inspired by the link found between low childhood vitamin D levels and mental health problems.

Almost 350 children were given either a dose of 10 µg or 30 µg of vitamin D from age 2 weeks until 2-years-old.

The results showed that at 6- to 8-years-old, almost 12 percent of children given 10 µg had significant internalising problems.

In the 30 µg group, though, this figure was under 6 percent.

No differences were seen in the number of externalising problems.

Externalising disorders include ADHD and conduct disorder.

Later in life externalising disorders include substance abuse, antisocial personality disorders and even psychopathy.

Dr Samuel Sandboge warned that the study has drawbacks:

“The results and their potential implications are interesting, but further research is needed to confirm the results.

In the interpretation of the results, we must note, among other things, that we studied the psychiatric symptoms only as parent-reported.

Furthermore, the participants of the study were children with Nordic ancestry living in Finland who had good levels of vitamin D.”

Around half the world’s population are thought to have an insufficiency of vitamin D, and 10 percent are deficient.

Vitamin D plays an important role in the development of the brain.

It is notable that a rise in autism and ADHD rates has happened at a time when there have been significant drops in average levels of vitamin D.

The study was published in JAMA Network Open (Sandboge et al., 2023).

#9722. Make Grilled Cheese Macedonian-Style For Double The Cheese & Flavor

Although less-famed than neighboring Greek and not-too-distant Turkish cooking, Northern Macedonian cuisine contains an abundance of delicious offerings. A mix of Balkan, Slavic, Mediterranean, and Middle Eastern influences, there's a lot to take from this regional culinary style. You can even infuse a Macedonian flair into grilled cheese by making a dish called przeni lepcinja.

Reminiscent of French toast but with a distinctly Mediterranean flair, this meal makes for a savvy way to use stale bread. Thick slices of bread — typically sourdough — are soaked in an egg and milk mixture, then layered with a generous dose of shredded mozzarella in between. This sandwich is then pan-fried in aromatic olive oil, thereby forming a golden-brown, bready dish, stuffed with gooey cheese inside. Scattered with feta atop before serving, it's an international grilled cheese style worth trying.

After all, feta and eggs are a tried-and-true pairing; the cheese is salty and tangy and adds a complex dimension to breakfast food. Meanwhile, that interior mozz melts down into creamy-gooey goodness that's still quintessentially a grilled cheese. The dish comes together with pantry staples, but presents the elements in a creative new form.

The classic przeni lepcinja formula is delicious, but the dish welcomes other components, too. Cheese is an important part of Macedonian cuisine – as well as Balkan food broadly — so tracking down regional cheese varieties can give your przeni lepcinja an extra-flavorful flair. Look out for belo sirenje, a crumbly white cheese reminiscent of feta, but crafted according to Macedonian techniques. Often made with sheep's milk, you can substitute it with Greek Sheep Milk Feta, a product that's easier to find in the United States.

Don't rule out enhancing the Macedonian grilled cheese stuffing, either. Chop up some tomatoes and peppers for a touch of sweetness. Or add some ajvar, a relish made with roasted eggplants and bell peppers. The condiment is also popular in Macedonia, and oftentimes served alongside cheese. Finally, round out your przeni lepcinja with ham, which will add both salt and meatiness to the dish. If the components are difficult to fit alongside the mozzarella, scoop out some of the bread's interior — the egg binder will hold the sandwich together. Flavorful and easy-to-make, przeni lepcinja is worth including in the weeknight rotation.

#9719. The Best Non-Traditional Chain Restaurant Reuben Sandwich, According To Customers

Reuben sandwiches, a throwback from the 1950s, are as closely linked to St. Patrick's Day as shamrocks and pots of gold, but you certainly don't have to wait until the March holiday to enjoy the salty, cheesy bite. There are, in fact, a number of chain restaurants that have Reubens on their menus year round, and in fact, Food Republic did a round-up of the 10 very best. Among the Arby's option, with its New York-style recipe, and Culver's grilled version, stuffed with meat, there is one standout choice that actually isn't super traditional, but customers love it anyway, and it's from Schlotzsky's Deli.

The Texas-based sandwich shop, which first opened its doors in 1971 has since grown to include nearly 300 locations across the U.S. This tasty Reuben is on the restaurant's permanent menu and what sets it apart from all the others is the bread. You see, while it has all the other markings of a classic Reuben, like pastrami, melted Swiss, a heap of sauerkraut, and Thousand Island Dressing (the other traditional option is Russian dressing, which is a little spicier), customers have the option of eating these ingredients on the chain's signature round sourdough. One reviewer on Google even proclaimed that they drive 40 minutes to get to the nearest Schlotzsky's to get its Reuben on this tangy white bread.

The deli sandwich chain does offer a rye option, which the customers love. But even Schlotzsky's dark rye bread is different from classic rye.

Schlotzsky's bread is so special that the Food Republic article cited customers as raving about it almost separate from all the fillings in its sandwiches. And the reason is simple: Unlike, say, McDonald's, whose English muffins are shipped in from a variety of regional bakeries, Schlotzsky's bread is baked fresh daily, in-house, and the employees do not cut any corners. Just like at home, the loaves at this chain must rise, proof, and then finally bake, in a process that takes about an hour (it is speeded up a bit by the use of in-kitchen proofers, which can accelerate the entire procedure).

But it's not just the freshness of the bread, it's also the ingredients, namely the proprietary sourdough starter that forms the basis of every bread the restaurant offers, from its Harvest Wheat, to the pizza crusts, and yes, even its rye bread. This is one part of what makes the Reuben from Schlotzsky's nontraditional, because aside from the fact that you can choose any of the chain's breads to fill with pastrami, cheese, sauerkraut and dressing, if you do opt for the rye bread, it isn't a classic, dense rye. Rather, it falls in line with the chain's sourdough, which is crispy on the outside but airy and tender on the inside, and is baked in a distinctive round shape.

#9716. The Spicy Sauce That Turns Beef Sandwiches Into A Baltimore Classic

There are plenty of reasons to take a trip to Baltimore; perhaps you're a fan of Old Bay seasoning and want to visit the place where its story began, or maybe you're eager to try Maryland's world-famous blue crabs. While Baltimore certainly doesn't lack options when it comes to seafood, the state is also home to a seriously impressive sandwich: pit beef. Made with thinly sliced, smoky roast beef piled onto a kaiser roll along with raw white onions, no pit beef is complete without a generous dollop of spicy tiger sauce.

Baltimore tiger sauce, a controversial inductee amongst regional barbecue sauces, requires just two core ingredients: mayonnaise and horseradish. Lemon juice, garlic, salt, and pepper are also common additions. Thanks to the horseradish, the sauce brings a different kind of burn than you get from chili peppers. When the root is grated or crushed, naturally occurring compounds called glucosinolates break down into pungent substances, including allyl isothiocyanate, which stimulates the same sensory receptors responsible for the sharp, biting sensation you get from wasabi — you know, the kind that hurts in the best way possible.

This sharp pungency helps cut through the richness of the smoky beef, and it's a great example of how a sandwich made with just a smattering of ingredients can still deliver complex flavors without needing to be piled high with a mismatch of toppings. A fresh batch can be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to two days, and you can use it for more than just pit beef sandwiches; try spreading it on other roast beef sandwiches, serving it alongside steak, or using it as a dipping sauce for fries when regular old mayo just isn't cutting it.

If you don't want your nose tingling and your eyes watering the entire time you're eating your pit beef, you'll need to go easy on the horseradish. Even a small amount packs a hefty punch, especially when fresh. For a milder, more manageable kick, reach for prepared horseradish instead. This condiment is made from freshly grated or ground horseradish root mixed with vinegar and salt, and pairing it with mayo helps tame some of its harsh pungency. As a frame of reference, start without about one tablespoon of prepared horseradish for every quarter cup of mayonnaise, then taste and gradually add more until you reach your preferred level of punchiness.

But there's one element even more important than the tiger sauce, and that's the beef itself. There's plenty of debate over which cut works best, although most roads lead to either top round or bottom round. Both come from the cow's hindquarters, making them relatively lean cuts that are well-suited to pit beef. Traditionally, the meat is cooked over a hot charcoal fire, developing that smoky, browned crust while the inside stays pink and juicy. At home, a gas grill or even a hot cast iron skillet can get the job done if you don't have a charcoal grill handy.

Since these cuts don't have much fat to keep them moist, take care not to overcook them, or you'll end up with tough, dry beef. Once the roast has rested, grab the sharpest knife you own and slice the beef as thinly as possible (always against the grain). Those wafer-thin slices are key to getting that signature Baltimore pit beef sandwich texture.

#9713. The Clothes That Make People Appear More Intelligent

How to use clothes to appear more competent.

How to use clothes to appear more competent.

Wearing more clothing makes you look more competent, a study finds.

Something as simple as taking off a sweater is enough to make you look less competent, the researchers found.

The finding applies to both men and women, said Dr Kurt Gray, the study’s first author:

“An important thing about our study is that, unlike much previous research, ours applies to both sexes.

It also calls into question the nature of objectification because people without clothes are not seen as mindless objects, but they are instead attributed a different kind of mind.”

The effect occurs because seeing more flesh encourages us to think about a person’s body, rather than their mind.

“We also show that this effect can happen even without the removal of clothes.

Simply focusing on someone’s attractiveness, in essence concentrating on their body rather than their mind, makes you see her or him as less of an agent [someone who acts and plans] more of an experiencer.”

Showing bare skin, though, does have some advantages, explained Dr Gray:

“A focus on the body, and the increased perception of sensitivity and emotion it elicits might be good for lovers in the bedroom.

Others appear to be less inclined to harm people with bare skin and more inclined to protect them.

In one experiment, for example, people viewing male subjects with their shirts off were less inclined to give those subjects uncomfortable electric shocks than when the men had their shirts on.”

“Even more than robbing someone of agency, the increased experience that may accompany body perceptions may lead those who are characterized in terms of their bodies to be seen as more reactive and emotional, traits that may also serve to work against career advancement.”

The study was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (Gray et al., 2011).
